title: Thank the emperor
hookLine: Marcus wrote to no one and ended up writing to everyone

lines: A TENT ON THE FRONTIER, AFTER DARK.
cards: A tent on the Danube frontier, sometime in the 170s, after dark. The man inside is the emperor of Rome, and he is writing in a private notebook, in Greek, to nobody. Not to the Senate.
Not to his son. To himself. Get up, there's work to do.
You'll meet difficult people today. You're getting angry again. Nobody was meant to read it.
Today it sits on nightstands and in backpacks around the world. The last of three thank-yous.

teach.b: First, a notebook with no reader. Marcus Aurelius ruled Rome from 161 to 180, and spent much of his last decade at war in the north.
Two of the books carry small notes of where they were written: among the Quadi, by the river Granua, and at Carnuntum, an army base on the Danube. He never mentions publishing.
He talks to himself as you, the way you talk to yourself in the car. Second, how close it came to vanishing. After his death the notebook goes almost silent in the record for centuries.

teach.h: ARETHAS AND A WORN OLD COPY.
teach.b: Around the year 900, a Byzantine bishop named Arethas writes in a letter that he owns an old copy, worn and battered. The first printed edition came out in 1559, from a manuscript that is now lost.
A private book, hanging by a thread. Third, why it reaches everyone.
He wasn't performing. A speech has to look good; a note to yourself only has to be true. So Marcus admits things.
Again and again he tells himself to stop getting angry. In book eight he orders himself: let no one hear you complaining about life at court any more, not even you.
The ruler of an empire, caught grumbling, and catching himself.
Book one is itself a page of thanks: to his grandfather, his mother, his teachers, his adoptive father, and the gods, each for something specific.
So the fitting thanks is his own kind: name one specific thing he gave you. For many readers it's this: you can talk to yourself firmly and kindly, in plain words, and get up again.

how: Many readers of the Meditations keep a private notebook of their own, writing short lines to themselves in the second person, the way Marcus did.

o: Marcus's son, the notebook's first intended reader
the bishop who owned a worn copy of Marcus's notebook
the scribe who first printed the notebook in 1559

games.q: to himself, to us — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus wrote the Meditations for the public
he never mentions a reader; he writes to himself, as you.
Marcus wrote his notebook in Greek
Greek, the language of philosophy for educated Romans.
the notebook was well-known right after his death
it goes almost silent for centuries; Arethas mentions an old copy around 900.

games.q: you're Marcus, alone in a tent on the frontier at night. who do you write to?
games.why: himself: the notebook talks to 'you' and never mentions publishing. that's exactly why it later spoke to everyone.

practice: Think of one thing you've needed to hear lately, not a slogan but something specific, the way Marcus wrote: you're tired, so rest before you answer.
Write it as one plain, kind line to yourself, on your phone or the back of a receipt, and read it once, slowly. You don't have to show anyone; he didn't.

wordCard.voice: Arethas, the Byzantine bishop who, around the year 900, owned a worn old copy of Marcus's private notebook, keeping it alive for us to read. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: grace, favor, and thanks, one word for the gift and the gratitude it calls up.

carryVoice: Your line: to himself, to us. A note meant for no one can still find its way to you. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Meditations, notes at the end of book 1 and the start of book 3 (the Quadi, the Granua, Carnuntum)
Arethas of Caesarea, letter to Demetrius of Heraclea (c. 907)
